title: Classification and Uses of Finger Prints
author: Sir Edward Richard Henry (1850–1931)
publisher: London: George Routledge and Sons, Limited
plate_used: Section “ILLUSTRATIONS”, sub-plate “Tracing the Ridges—Meeting”, print no. 139 (a whorl pattern), book page ~133
holding_institution: U.S. National Library of Medicine (digitised copy; Medical Heritage Library / Internet Archive)
source_file_used: https://archive.org/download/1306026.nlm.nih.gov/1306026.pdf (page image for print no. 139, rendered at high resolution from the archived PDF)
licence_evidence: Published 1900 in London; author Edward Richard Henry died in 1931, so the work is public domain under the Swiss rule of 70 years post mortem auctoris (expired 2001) as well as under UK/EU term (life+70, expired 2001).

The item is catalogued by the U.S. National Library of Medicine and hosted on the Internet Archive in the 'medicalheritagelibrary' / 'usnationallibraryofmedicine' collections with no copyright restriction recorded; it was published well before 1929 and so is also in the public domain in the United States.

A parallel Google Books digitisation of the same 1900 edition, archive.org identifier 'classificationa00henrgoog' (https://archive.org/details/classificationa00henrgoog), carries the explicit Internet Archive metadata field possible-copyright-status: NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, independently corroborating the public-domain status of this exact book and edition.
how_used: The published PDF page containing illustration print no. 139 (a clean inked whorl impression, part of the book's own ridge-tracing teaching plate) was rendered from the archived PDF at high resolution (scripts/weekly_poster_w47_print.py was NOT used to re-derive this at runtime; the extraction was done once, offline, by a one-off script, and only its numeric output is shipped as data). The scan was binarised and skeletonised (own Zhang-Suen thinning implementation, numpy only) to recover the real centre-lines of the printed ridges, and a distance transform (iterative erosion, numpy only) gave each centre-line point the scan's own real local ink thickness, smoothed with a 7-point moving average and clamped to a narrow range so a ridge tapers rather than beads. Those centre-lines were traced into polylines. A handful of scan artefacts -- the printed plate's own table-rule line (a long, almost perfectly straight run along one edge of the scan) and a few similarly long, near-perfectly-straight runs no real whorl ridge makes, found by straightness and position -- were dropped, along with short, near-straight bridges directly joining two otherwise-unconnected junctions (scan noise bridging two adjacent ridges). The remaining real ridges were merged/split (never invented, and no width or position was invented either) so that there are exactly 974 ridge-line segments — one per new decision in week 47 — each still carrying its own real per-point width, ordered by distance from the whorl's own core and assigned to three ink plates by language band (40 innermost = Italian, next 381 = French, outer 553 = German). The resulting polyline coordinates and widths (no raster image, no photograph) are stored in segments_974.json and drawn by weekly_poster_w47_print.py as a simulated risograph/screenprint: three vivid ink plates (ultramarine/vermilion/fluorescent yellow), each offset a few px for plate misregistration and textured with its own procedural grain (an SVG filter, not a scan-resampled bitmap -- noted here for accuracy), overprinted with a multiply blend onto a fourth plate, the huge '974' itself in dense ink. The page is scaled to contain the whole print -- never to crop it, asserted in code (every one of the 974 segments keeps >=90% of its own length on the page) -- so the ridges touch the top, left and right edges, and the print's own aspect leaves a little room below that the '974' plate itself fills edge to edge. Nothing in the artwork was procedurally drawn in the sense of invented geometry — every stroke, including its thickness and position, follows a real ridge traced from the 1900 scan; only the ink-grain texture is a synthetic approximation of print noise, not resampled from the scan.
extraction_note: segments_974.json is derived data (polyline coordinates only), produced once from the scan above by an offline script; the scan itself is not redistributed in this repository.
